title: Slavery in the law, honestly
hookLine: the books that say love your neighbor also regulate slavery; some laws limit it, some are hard to read, and Christians read them in different ways

lines: WHY DOES THE BIBLE ALLOW SLAVERY?
cards: A teenager posts a question online: why does the Bible allow slavery? Some replies explain it away. Some defend it.
The reply with the most votes says only that it's disturbing to watch people justify it. So here it is, straight.
The laws of Moses, the same books that say love your neighbor as yourself and proclaim liberty in the jubilee, also regulate slavery. Today's word is the Hebrew for servant, or slave.

teach.b: Ebed. In Hebrew it can mean servant, worker or slave, and the context decides. Moses himself is called the ebed of the LORD.
But in these laws it often means a person owned by another. Some of the laws limit it.

teach.h: IN THE SEVENTH HE SHALL GO OUT FREE.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free."
He's to be sent off with gifts, and the reason is given: "thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt." Another law forbids handing an escaped slave back to his master.
Kidnapping a person to sell carried the death penalty. Other laws are hard to read. Foreigners could be bought, and "they shall be your bondmen for ever."
A master who beats a slave who survives a day or two goes unpunished, "for he is his money." Honest readers don't pretend that's gentle. So how do Christians read these pages?
Some point to the ancient world, where slavery was everywhere, and see these laws as limits on it, a first step.
Some point to Jesus, who said Moses allowed divorce "because of the hardness of your hearts," and read the slavery laws the same way: allowed, not blessed.
Some say plainly that these laws reflect their writers' world, not God's will for any time. Jewish readers have their own long tradition of wrestling with them too.
And in nineteenth-century America, both sides quoted the Bible. Defenders of slavery quoted these laws and Paul.

Abolitionists quoted the kidnapping law, the image of God in every person, and Paul's "neither bond nor free." The same law that regulates the ebed begins with slaves in Egypt crying out, and being heard.

how: Christians read the Old Testament's slavery laws in different ways: as limits on an ancient practice, as concessions to hardness of heart, or as human words of their time. Churches today teach that slavery is a grave wrong, and many point to the image of God in every person.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a Hebrew servant goes out free

s: the law of Moses says nothing about slavery
it regulates it: some laws limit it, and some are hard to read.
one law forbids handing an escaped slave back to his master
it's in Deuteronomy, one of the laws that pushes against the system.
in the 1800s only slavery's defenders quoted the Bible
abolitionists quoted it too: the kidnapping law, the image of God, "neither bond nor free."

games.q: a friend reads Exodus 21 for the first time and says: this is awful. what do you do?
o: agree it's hard, and share how different readers wrestle with it.
tell them to skip that part.
games.why: honest readers say it plainly: "for he is his money" is hard to read. then they show how they wrestle with it, without defending it or skipping it.

practice: Let one hard line sit in front of you: for he is his money. Don't explain it; let it be as hard as it is, and hold, with respect, the people who lived under words like these.
If you pray, bring the verse to God, the way Israel cried out in Egypt; if you don't, simply stay honest with it.
